description:
ASTRAWORKS is a team of curious minds who enjoy exploring ideas, solving problems, and turning concepts into something meaningful.

We bring together different perspectives, skills, and interests, with a shared passion for science, technology, and innovation. We believe the best solutions come from collaboration, and the willingness to think beyond conventional approaches

For us, it's not just about competing; it's about exploring possibilities and building something worth sharing.
summary:
Earth Jukebox: Pakistan turns NASA climate data into music, so people can hear climate change, not just see it. Choose a city and press play: each month from 1981 to 2025 lasts 2.5 seconds, while a 3D map shows the same weather you hear.

Data: NASA POWER temperature and rainfall, NASA MODIS greenery, USGS earthquakes, and World Bank CMIP6 projections to 2090. We compute the drought index from NASA rainfall.

Why we made these choices: raw numbers sound like noise, so every note is forced onto the A minor scale at a steady tempo. Our own “climate stress” index drives a film-score build, from a calm drone to strings and low pulsing beats. Each category has its own instrument: glass chimes for heat, rain drops for rain, dry wind for drought, a deep boom for earthquakes.

The emotion is the point. The 2022 Karachi flood fills the music with rain, the 2005 Islamabad earthquake breaks the calm, and the future mode lets listeners hear 2090 grow hotter.

Accessibility is built in: spoken updates, screen-reader descriptions, high contrast and keyboard control.
details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Jukebox: Pakistan turns NASA Earth data into music you can explore. You start in space, the globe zooms into Pakistan, and you pick one of five cities: Karachi, Quetta, Lahore, Islamabad or Peshawar. Press play and each month from 1981 to 2025 lasts 2.5 seconds. The city’s ground rises out of the map in its own shape, and the weather you see matches the numbers you hear: clouds, rain, storms, drought dust, heat, and cracks and shaking for earthquakes. A “Sound of the data” display shows which instrument is sounding, so you can see how the data becomes sound.

How the sound is made
Raw numbers sound like noise, so every note is forced onto the A minor scale at a steady tempo. A “climate stress” index (our own blend of heat, rain, drought and earthquakes) drives a film-score build, from a calm drone to strings and low pulsing beats. Each category has its own instrument: glass chimes for heat, rain drops for rain, dry wind for drought, and a deep boom for earthquakes. Every value is compared with that month’s normal, so ordinary months stay gentle and extreme months stand out.

Extra features
Compare two cities, with one in each ear. Hear NASA-based temperature projections to 2090 for two scenarios, always labelled “projection, not a measurement”. Use the history chart to jump to any month.

Benefits and intended impact
Earth science is mostly shown as pictures, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. We want climate data to be something people can hear and feel, so it is easier to understand and remember. Accessibility is built in: spoken updates, screen-reader descriptions of every month, high contrast, a calm-motion switch, keyboard control, and a word beside every colour. It also works offline, so it can be used in classrooms with little internet.

Data
NASA POWER (temperature and rainfall), NASA MODIS (greenery), NASA GIBS (map pictures), USGS (earthquakes) and the World Bank CMIP6 projections. We compute the drought index (SPI) from NASA rainfall. Every number has a named source, and nothing is invented.

Tools
JavaScript, React, Vite, Electron (desktop app) and MapLibre GL (the 3D globe). Tone.js makes the music, and Python scripts prepared the data and shapes. It runs on a normal Windows computer or in a modern browser, with no special hardware. Headphones are best. We tested it with 147 automated tests. AI coding assistants (Gemini) helped us write code; the team chose the idea, data, sound design and testing.

What makes it creative, and what we considered
We chose to be honest and musical at the same time. We show data limits openly, avoid flashing lights (lightning never flashes more than once every 4 seconds), and let people turn motion off. We also kept the weather simple enough for young people, and made sure each sound means something you can check against the numbers.
dataRefs: NASA POWER: monthly temperature and rainfall (T2M, PRECTOTCORR)
NASA MODIS MOD13A3 monthly vegetation index (NDVI), via AppEEARS
NASA GIBS: Blue Marble Shaded Relief with Bathymetry (globe imagery)
NASA GIBS: Landsat WELD Corrected Reflectance True Colour, 1990 (city close-ups)
NASA Earthdata (account used for the downloads)
projectRefs: USGS Earthquake Catalog (ComCat), magnitude 4.5 and up within 300 km of each city
World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal: CMIP6 temperature projections (SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5)
Natural Earth: country borders and coastlines
MapLibre GL JS: the 3D globe and map (open source)
React, Vite, Zustand, Electron, Vitest: app tools (open source)
Fontsource: Bricolage Grotesque, Figtree and Spline Sans Mono fonts
